levels.title: Licensing only wants rows that line up
levels.task: Ops just added a second table, album_info: each row has the album name and label. The chart desk’s licensing contact wants to see all the information from the top_songs and album_info tables joined together.
levels.solution: SELECT * FROM top_songs JOIN album_info ON top_songs.album_name = album_info.album_name;
levels.hintMessage: JOIN the top_songs and album_info tables on the album_name column.
levels.successMessage: Great job! You joined the two tables on the album_name column and selected all the columns from both tables.

levels.title: Marketing analytics needs one number
levels.task: Someone on the festival marketing squad is sanity-checking the chart. They only care about albums that have a label
levels.solution: SELECT * FROM top_songs INNER JOIN album_info ON top_songs.album_name = album_info.album_name;
levels.hintMessage: INNER JOIN the top_songs and album_info tables on the album_name column.
levels.successMessage: Great job! You joined the two tables for albums that have a label.

levels.title: Tour liaison needs the full list, gaps and all
levels.task: Road office is building a day-of binder. For ids 1001 through 1005 they want every training-chart track listed with whatever label name we have on file—if we have nothing, the label side should simply be empty. First column: track name. Second column title must read label.
levels.solution:
SELECT t.track_name, a.label AS label
FROM top_songs t
LEFT JOIN album_info a ON t.album_name = a.album_name
WHERE t.id BETWEEN 1001 AND 1005;
levels.hintMessage: Start from the chart slice, attach directory rows where album names match, and alias the label column as label.
levels.successMessage: Five lines on the sheet—exactly what routing asked for.

levels.title: Show ops double-checks the widened list
levels.task: Programming lead wants proof the “don’t drop anyone” version of that same join still returns five lines for ids 1001–1005—not three, not six. One column only, named left_join_rows, equal to the row count.
levels.solution:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS left_join_rows
FROM top_songs t
LEFT JOIN album_info a ON t.album_name = a.album_name
WHERE t.id BETWEEN 1001 AND 1005;
levels.hintMessage: Use the same chart-to-directory pairing as the tour sheet, then count every row in the result.
levels.successMessage: Five rows—show ops can green-light the run of show.

levels.title: Royalty audit: who never hit the directory?
levels.task: Finance partner on the royalty desk is chasing missing paperwork. From the same training-chart ids (1001–1005), they want only the tracks that still have no matching row in the label directory. Output just track_name, ordered alphabetically by album name (so the binder lines up with how they sort physical LPs).
levels.solution:
SELECT t.track_name
FROM top_songs t
LEFT JOIN album_info a ON t.album_name = a.album_name
WHERE t.id BETWEEN 1001 AND 1005
  AND a.album_name IS NULL
ORDER BY t.album_name;
levels.hintMessage: Widen to the directory first, then keep rows where the directory side never matched. Sort using the chart’s album column.
levels.successMessage: Those two names go straight to the follow-up queue.
